name: Programme Essentials
description: The Programme Essentials baseline establishes the foundational framework for managing coordinated multi-project initiatives that deliver strategic benefits through cross-project orchestration, benefits realization, and organizational transformation.

focuses.name: Value
focuses.description: Addresses why the programme exists, for whom, and how it creates and confirms strategic benefits -- encompassing the strategic investment thesis, programme-level stakeholder ecosystem, and benefits realization throughout the programme lifecycle.

focuses.name: Solution
focuses.description: Addresses what the programme is trying to achieve and produce -- encompassing strategic outcomes, integrated programme capabilities, and the target organizational state defined by the blueprint.

focuses.name: Endeavor
focuses.description: Addresses how the programme is organized and executed -- encompassing team-of-teams formation, programme-level coordination work, and the programme operating model.

focuses.name: Coordination
focuses.description: Addresses how related projects are synchronized, sequenced, governed, and orchestrated toward shared strategic outcomes -- encompassing the programme as a managed entity, strategic roadmap sequencing, cross-project dependency management, and programme-level governance oversight.

narrativeTypes.name: The STAR Format
narrativeTypes.description: A structured storytelling framework for tactical programme execution reporting, case studies, and lessons learned documentation. Use when communicating specific programme experiences, coordination achievements, or retrospective insights that need clear situational context and measurable outcomes.

narrativeElements.name: Situation
narrativeElements.description: The programme context and conditions that set the stage for the narrative.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the programme environment, organizational context, multi-project complexity, and relevant circumstances that existed before the intervention. Include enough detail to establish programme-level starting conditions without unnecessary elaboration. At programme level, this includes the number of teams, strategic context, and governance landscape.

narrativeElements.name: Task
narrativeElements.description: The specific programme challenge or responsibility that needed to be addressed within the situation.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Articulate the concrete cross-project goal, coordination challenge, or programme mandate that drove action. Connect the task to strategic objectives, benefit realization targets, or governance requirements. Be specific about what programme-level success would look like and what constraints applied.

narrativeElements.name: Action
narrativeElements.description: The specific coordination steps, governance decisions, and programme-level interventions taken to address the task.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe what was actually done at the programme level, by which roles, and how. Focus on cross-project decisions, dependency resolution approaches, and stakeholder engagement strategies. Include collaboration aspects across teams and alternatives considered.

narrativeElements.name: Result
narrativeElements.description: The measurable programme outcomes, benefits delivered, and lessons produced by the actions taken.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Quantify results using programme-level metrics: benefit realization data, predictability improvements, dependency resolution rates, stakeholder satisfaction scores. Include both intended and unintended outcomes. Capture lessons learned and connect results back to the original programme objectives.

narrativeTypes.name: The Hero's Journey
narrativeTypes.description: A transformation lifecycle narrative for communicating major organizational or programme change journeys. Use for strategic communications, executive presentations, change management narratives, and organizational storytelling that convey the full arc of a programme transformation from inception to realized benefits.

narrativeElements.name: The Ordinary World
narrativeElements.description: The pre-programme organizational state -- the current environment, established practices, and status quo before transformation.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Paint a clear, honest picture of the pre-programme state that stakeholders will recognize as authentic. Document existing capabilities alongside limitations, established ways of working alongside their constraints. Establish measurable baselines against which programme transformation will be measured. At programme level, this includes the organizational structure, process landscape, and capability gaps that the programme will address.

narrativeElements.name: The Call to Adventure
narrativeElements.description: The strategic catalyst that triggers the programme -- the opportunity identified, the business case established, or the strategic vision compelling coordinated change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Articulate what made the status quo untenable or what opportunity was compelling enough to justify multi-project investment. Connect to the programme opportunity and business case. Create urgency by quantifying the cost of inaction alongside the potential of coordinated programme delivery. Identify key sponsors and what they stood to gain.

narrativeElements.name: The Ordeal
narrativeElements.description: The cross-project challenges, organizational resistance, dependency conflicts, and pivotal moments encountered during programme delivery that test the team-of-teams and approach.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe significant programme-level challenges honestly -- cross-team dependency crises, organizational change resistance, governance pivots when assumptions proved wrong, benefit realization shortfalls that required adaptation. Show how the programme adapted through cadence-based coordination, governance intervention, and stakeholder re-engagement. Include at least one genuine programme-level crisis or turning point.

narrativeElements.name: The Return
narrativeElements.description: The transformed organizational state -- benefits realized, capabilities embedded, new operating model established, and ongoing sustainment confirmed.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Contrast the post-programme reality with the Ordinary World using the same baselines. Quantify benefit realization against the original business case. Highlight sustainable organizational changes that will outlast the programme. Acknowledge remaining challenges and residual risks to maintain credibility.

narrativeTypes.name: Micro-Narratives (ABT)
narrativeTypes.description: A concise storytelling framework for programme status updates, governance communications, and brief decision requests. Use when communicating programme status, escalating cross-project issues, or requesting governance decisions in formats needing essential information in minimal time.

narrativeElements.name: And (Context)
narrativeElements.description: The established programme facts, current delivery status, and shared understanding forming the communication's foundation.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State relevant programme context briefly, referencing what governance stakeholders already know about programme status, current tranche progress, and benefit realization trajectory. Establish shared understanding without repeating unnecessary detail. Keep to 1-2 sentences.

narrativeElements.name: But (Conflict)
narrativeElements.description: The cross-project complication, dependency risk, or strategic challenge requiring governance attention.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the specific programme-level tension that makes this communication necessary: a critical dependency threatening delivery, a benefit realization shortfall requiring intervention, or a strategic alignment concern. Quantify impact on programme objectives where possible. Keep to 1-2 sentences.

narrativeElements.name: Therefore (Resolution)
narrativeElements.description: The proposed programme action, governance recommendation, or strategic decision request addressing the conflict.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State clearly what governance decision is requested, what programme response is proposed, or what strategic adjustment is recommended. If requesting a governance decision, present options with a clear recommendation tied to benefit realization and strategic alignment. Keep to 1-3 sentences.

narrativeTypes.name: PDCA
narrativeTypes.description: A continuous improvement framework for programme retrospectives, coordination process improvement, and operating model refinement. Use when documenting iterative improvement cycles for programme coordination practices, governance processes, or team-of-teams effectiveness.

narrativeElements.name: Plan
narrativeElements.description: Analysis of current programme coordination situation, identification of improvement opportunities, and design of the intervention.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Document observations through programme-level data and cross-team feedback. State the improvement hypothesis: "We believe a specific coordination change will result in measurable programme improvement because of a stated rationale." Define success criteria with measurable targets (e.g., dependency resolution rate, planning event effectiveness, cross-team lead time).

narrativeElements.name: Do
narrativeElements.description: Execution of the planned improvement within a defined programme increment or tranche.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe implementation noting which coordination mechanisms, governance processes, or operating model elements were modified. Document observations during the trial period including cross-team reactions and unexpected side effects. Note deviations from plan and reasons.

narrativeElements.name: Check
narrativeElements.description: Evaluation of results against the plan using programme-level metrics and cross-team feedback.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Compare actual programme results to success criteria. Analyze quantitative data (flow metrics, predictability measures, benefit realization progress) and qualitative feedback from teams and governance bodies. Distinguish correlation from causation in programme-level improvement.

narrativeElements.name: Act
narrativeElements.description: Decision to adopt, adapt, or abandon the improvement based on evidence, and standardization of successful changes in the programme operating model.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Make an explicit decision: adopt into the programme operating model, adapt for the next increment, or abandon with documented rationale. If adopting, update coordination agreements and governance processes. If adapting, design the next iteration. Update the programme improvement backlog.

narrativeTypes.name: Lifecycle
narrativeTypes.description: A prerequisite-gated progression framework for documenting sequential programme phase transitions, tranche boundaries, and gated governance decisions. Use when communicating structured programme progressions where each phase has defined entry criteria and governance gates.

narrativeElements.name: Prerequisites
narrativeElements.description: Conditions, criteria, or prior states that must be satisfied before the programme phase or tranche can begin.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Define specific, verifiable entry criteria with enough precision for objective governance confirmation. Reference programme concern states (e.g., Programme Governance at "Established" state), completed governance reviews, or benefit realization thresholds. Distinguish mandatory prerequisites from recommended prerequisites. Include the "desirable, viable, achievable" test from MSP at each gateway.

narrativeElements.name: Lifecycle Phase
narrativeElements.description: Activities, milestones, and state transitions that occur within the programme phase or tranche, advancing concerns toward next states.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the programme coordination work that occurs, key governance decisions, and concern state transitions achieved during the tranche. Reference relevant activity spaces and concern states. Include guidance on typical tranche duration (6-12 months for MSP, 8-12 weeks for SAFe PI), resource needs, common challenges, and exit criteria for governance review.

narrativeTypes.name: Benefits Chain
narrativeTypes.description: A benefits realization storytelling framework for communicating how programme investment translates into strategic value through a traceable chain from project outputs through organizational capabilities and outcomes to measurable benefits. Use when presenting benefit realization plans to governance bodies, communicating the purpose of organizational change activities, or explaining why capability delivery alone is insufficient for value realization.

narrativeElements.name: Outputs
narrativeElements.description: The tangible deliverables and products produced by constituent projects within the programme.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the specific project deliverables (systems, tools, processes, documents) that are being produced. Be concrete and verifiable: "the new CRM system is deployed" rather than "technology is in place." Identify which constituent projects produce which outputs and confirm delivery status. Outputs are necessary but not sufficient -- they are the starting point of the benefits chain, not the endpoint.

narrativeElements.name: Capabilities
narrativeElements.description: The organizational abilities enabled by combining outputs with trained people, adapted processes, and organizational structures.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe what the organization can now do that it could not do before. Capabilities emerge when outputs are combined with organizational readiness: a deployed system becomes a capability only when staff are trained, processes are adapted, and organizational structures support its use. Identify the organizational change activities required to transform outputs into capabilities.

narrativeElements.name: Outcomes
narrativeElements.description: The measurable changes in organizational behavior, performance, or effectiveness that result from capability adoption.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the observable changes in how the organization operates: "customer orders are processed end-to-end digitally" rather than "the digital ordering capability exists." Outcomes require sustained adoption -- temporary behavior change does not constitute an outcome. Measure outcomes through operational metrics: process cycle times, error rates, adoption rates, customer satisfaction scores.

narrativeElements.name: Benefits
narrativeElements.description: The measurable improvements in strategic performance that stakeholders value and that justify the programme investment.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Quantify the strategic value delivered: revenue growth, cost reduction, market position improvement, regulatory compliance achievement, employee satisfaction gains. Benefits must be measured against the baselines established in the benefits realization plan. Connect back to the original business case to demonstrate return on investment. Identify any emergent benefits not originally planned and any dis-benefits that materialized.

narrativeTypes.name: Essay
narrativeTypes.description: A structured exposition framework for presenting comprehensive analysis, context, and conclusions about practice elements.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: The opening context that establishes the subject matter, its importance, and the scope of the narrative.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the concept and its significance to the practice without referencing the narrative structure itself. Establish why this element matters and what problem or need it addresses. Keep to 2-3 sentences.

narrativeElements.name: Body
narrativeElements.description: The substantive analysis providing detailed context, methodology guidance, and domain-specific insights.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Present the core content drawing from authoritative sources. Include practical guidance, key considerations, and domain-specific context. Reference specific methodologies, frameworks, and evidence. Keep to 3-5 sentences covering the most important points.

narrativeElements.name: Conclusion
narrativeElements.description: The synthesis connecting the analysis to practical outcomes and ongoing relevance.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Summarize the key insight and connect to practical outcomes. Emphasize the ongoing nature of the practice and its contribution to organizational capability. Keep to 2-3 sentences.

narrativeTypes.name: Technique
narrativeTypes.description: A structured how-to framework for documenting activity execution guidance, including context, step-by-step technique, and lessons from common failures.

narrativeElements.name: Overview
narrativeElements.description: The purpose and value proposition of the activity in the context of the practice.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State what this activity produces and why it matters to the practice's objectives. Connect to the alpha states it advances. Keep to 2-3 sentences focused on outcomes, not process.

narrativeElements.name: Technique
narrativeElements.description: The detailed how-to guidance for performing the activity effectively.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the specific steps, methods, and approaches for performing this activity. Reference established techniques, frameworks, and tools. Include enough detail that a practitioner could follow the guidance without external references. Keep focused on actionable guidance.

narrativeElements.name: Common Pitfalls
narrativeElements.description: The most frequent mistakes and anti-patterns observed when performing this activity.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Identify 3-4 specific failure modes that practitioners commonly encounter. For each pitfall, describe what goes wrong and why it is problematic. Focus on preventable errors rather than environmental factors outside the team's control.

competencies.name: Analysis
competencies.description: The ability to understand complex programme-level situations, assess strategic options, evaluate evidence across multiple projects, and transform organizational opportunities into actionable programme inputs.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Can gather information using standard techniques, document findings in structured formats, and assist with programme-level analysis under guidance. Understands fundamental analytical concepts such as strategic assessment, benefits analysis, and dependency mapping but requires supervision for interpretation and synthesis across multiple projects.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can independently analyze programme-level situations, assess strategic options, evaluate cross-project risks, and produce structured analysis outputs. Applies analytical frameworks to programme planning and governance. Distinguishes between project-level symptoms and programme-level root causes.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can analyze complex, ambiguous programme situations with multiple competing priorities and stakeholder groups spanning organizational levels. Selects and adapts analytical techniques to programme context. Produces comprehensive programme analyses that drive strategic decision-making. Mentors others in programme-level analytical techniques.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can innovate analytical approaches for novel programme situations including multi-organizational contexts. Integrates quantitative and qualitative methods across multiple projects and domains. Anticipates analytical needs before they are articulated. Coaches teams and organizations in building programme-level analytical capability.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Creates new analytical frameworks, methodologies, and tools that advance organizational capability in programme analysis. Recognized as an authority on programme-level analysis within and beyond the organization. Shapes industry thinking on programme analytical approaches.

narratives.name: Building Analytical Capability from Data Collection to Strategic Foresight
narratives.description: Progression of programme-level analytical competency across five maturity levels.
citationNames: The Standard for Program Management -- Fourth Edition

narrativeContexts.context: Development of programme-level analytical competency requires foundational skills in structured information gathering, logical reasoning, and quantitative interpretation. Practitioners entering at the Basic level should understand that programme analysis operates at a qualitatively different level from project analysis, requiring synthesis across multiple projects, stakeholder groups, and organizational levels. Familiarity with strategic assessment techniques such as business case evaluation, benefits analysis, and dependency mapping provides the conceptual foundation, though application at programme scale requires guided experience. Organizational investment in mentoring relationships with experienced programme analysts and progressive exposure to cross-project analytical challenges accelerates competency development.

Analytical competency at programme level develops through progressive exposure to increasingly complex multi-project environments. Basic practitioners gather information using standard techniques and document findings in structured formats, requiring supervision for interpretation and synthesis across project boundaries. At the Applies level, practitioners independently analyze programme-level situations, assess strategic options, evaluate cross-project risks, and distinguish between project-level symptoms and programme-level root causes. Mastery emerges when practitioners can analyze complex, ambiguous situations with multiple competing priorities and stakeholder groups spanning organizational levels, selecting and adapting analytical techniques to programme context and producing analyses that drive strategic decision-making. The Adapts level represents the ability to innovate analytical approaches for novel multi-organizational contexts, integrating quantitative and qualitative methods across domains and anticipating analytical needs before they are articulated. At the Innovating level, practitioners create new analytical frameworks and methodologies that advance organizational capability in programme analysis and shape industry thinking on analytical approaches for coordinated multi-project delivery.

competencies.name: Leadership
competencies.description: The ability to inspire, guide, motivate, and empower people across multiple teams and organizational levels to achieve programme objectives through vision-setting, strategic decision-making, influence, coaching, and the creation of environments where teams-of-teams can perform at their best.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Can follow established leadership guidelines, support programme coordination, and contribute positively to team-of-teams dynamics. Understands basic programme leadership concepts such as strategic alignment, stakeholder management, and cross-team motivation but leads only in well-defined situations with clear guidance.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can lead work streams or coordination functions within a programme effectively. Provides clear direction across teams, makes routine cross-team decisions confidently, and supports programme coordination through facilitation and coaching. Applies situational leadership across diverse team contexts.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can lead complex programmes with multiple teams, diverse stakeholders, and challenging organizational environments. Adapts leadership style to different organizational levels and contexts. Navigates programme-level politics effectively. Creates psychological safety across a team-of-teams. Mentors emerging programme leaders.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can lead in highly uncertain, politically charged multi-organizational programme environments. Influences organizational strategy and culture through programme leadership example. Leads cross-organizational initiatives and develops programme leadership capability across the organization.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Shapes programme leadership practice within and beyond the organization. Creates innovative leadership models suited to team-of-teams and scaled delivery environments. Recognized as a thought leader in programme leadership. Influences industry-level standards and practices.

narratives.name: Developing Multi-Level Programme Direction from Team Guidance to Organizational Influence
narratives.description: Progression of programme leadership competency across five maturity levels.

narrativeContexts.context: Development of programme leadership competency requires foundational skills in interpersonal influence, decision-making under uncertainty, and the ability to motivate and empower people across diverse contexts. Practitioners entering at the Basic level should understand that programme leadership operates across multiple teams and organizational levels simultaneously, requiring servant-leadership principles that enable team-of-teams performance rather than command-and-control direction. Experience in leading individual teams or work streams provides essential grounding, but programme leadership demands additional capabilities in strategic alignment, cross-organizational negotiation, and the creation of psychological safety at scale. Organizational support through access to progressive leadership challenges, mentoring from experienced programme managers, and exposure to the political dynamics of multi-stakeholder environments accelerates competency development.

Programme leadership capability develops through progressive exposure to increasingly complex multi-team and multi-stakeholder environments. Basic practitioners follow established guidelines, support coordination, and contribute positively to team-of-teams dynamics in well-defined situations with clear guidance. At the Applies level, practitioners lead work streams or coordination functions effectively, providing clear direction across teams, making routine cross-team decisions, and applying situational leadership across diverse team contexts. Mastery emerges when practitioners can lead complex programmes with multiple teams and challenging organizational environments, adapting leadership style to different levels and contexts, navigating programme-level politics, and creating psychological safety across a team-of-teams. The Adapts level represents the ability to lead in highly uncertain, politically charged multi-organizational environments, influencing organizational strategy and culture through programme leadership example. At the Innovating level, practitioners shape programme leadership practice through creating innovative models suited to team-of-teams and scaled delivery environments, influencing industry-level standards.

competencies.name: Management
competencies.description: The ability to plan, organize, coordinate, and control the resources, activities, and processes across multiple projects needed to achieve programme objectives, encompassing cross-project planning, shared resource allocation, programme-level tracking, and governance administration.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Can perform basic programme planning and tracking tasks, maintain programme records, and support coordination activities under guidance. Understands fundamental programme management concepts such as dependency tracking, milestone management, and cross-project reporting but requires supervision for complex multi-project tasks.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can independently plan, track, and manage programme coordination activities for small-to-medium programmes. Applies standard programme management tools and techniques effectively. Manages shared resources, programme schedules, and programme-level budgets within defined parameters. Produces accurate programme status reports.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can manage complex programmes with significant uncertainty, multiple teams, and substantial budgets. Selects and adapts programme management approaches to context. Performs quantitative analysis of programme flow metrics, predictability, and benefit realization. Manages complex governance structures. Mentors other programme managers.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can manage portfolios of programmes across organizational boundaries. Integrates programme management approaches for novel situations (multi-site, multi-methodology, multi-vendor). Establishes organizational programme management standards and maturity improvement. Coaches at the organizational level.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Creates new programme management frameworks, methodologies, and tools that advance organizational capability in coordinated multi-project delivery. Recognized as an authority on programme management practice. Shapes industry standards and practices.

narratives.name: From Coordinated Projects to Realized Strategic Benefits
narratives.description: Traces the complete programme journey from the recognition that independent project management is insufficient for strategic value creation through coordinated delivery, organizational transformation, and confirmed benefit realization.
citationNames: The Standard for Program Management -- Fourth Edition

narrativeContexts.context: Organizations manage related projects independently, treating each as an isolated delivery effort with its own governance, team structure, and success criteria. Strategic opportunities requiring multi-project coordination are pursued through project portfolios where coordination is achieved through periodic reporting rather than active orchestration. Benefits that require integrated capability delivery across multiple projects go unrealized because no management structure exists to coordinate the transition from project outputs through organizational capabilities and outcomes to measurable strategic improvements. Team structures reflect organizational convenience rather than value flow optimization, and cross-project dependencies are managed reactively through escalation rather than proactively through structural design.

The recognition that strategic value creation at scale requires a qualitatively different management approach -- one that coordinates related projects toward shared outcomes, actively manages the benefits realization chain, governs the strategic investment thesis, and orchestrates organizational change across multiple business units simultaneously. MSP's insight that programmes exist to deliver benefits unattainable through individual project management, PMI's structuring of programme management around five performance domains, SAFe's creation of the Agile Release Train as a semi-permanent coordination vehicle, and Team Topologies' recognition that team structure fundamentally shapes delivery outcomes all converge on this recognition: programme management is not "bigger project management" but a distinct discipline addressing qualitatively different challenges.

Programme implementation encounters the defining challenges of multi-project coordination: cross-team dependencies that create cascading delivery blockages; organizational change resistance from stakeholders who prefer established ways of working; governance tensions between oversight rigor and coordination agility; the persistent gap between capability delivery and benefit realization that threatens the return on investment; team-of-teams coordination overhead that consumes resources without proportionate value; and the multi-year timescale challenge of sustaining organizational commitment through leadership transitions, strategic pivots, and change fatigue. These challenges test whether the programme's coordination mechanisms, governance structures, and team-of-teams organization can deliver integrated value rather than merely adding management overhead to what could have been achieved through independent project delivery.

The programme delivers measurable strategic benefits that demonstrably could not have been achieved through independent project management. Integrated capabilities are deployed and operational, organizational change is embedded in business-as-usual operations, and benefit realization confirms the strategic investment thesis articulated in the original business case. The team-of-teams has evolved through the programme lifecycle, developing coordination capabilities that persist beyond the programme as organizational learning. Governance structures have been refined through PDCA cycles, producing an effective oversight model that balances assurance with agility. The programme operating model is documented as an organizational asset for reuse, and lessons about programme management -- from team topology design through benefits realization chain management to governance optimization -- improve the organization's capability to pursue similar strategic initiatives in the future.

competencies.name: Stakeholder Representation
competencies.description: The ability to identify, understand, represent, and balance the needs of diverse stakeholder groups across strategic, programme, project, and operational levels through multi-level engagement, expectation management, advocacy, negotiation, and the bridging of perspectives to achieve aligned programme direction.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Can identify programme stakeholder groups using standard templates, gather requirements across organizational levels, and document stakeholder needs. Understands that programme stakeholders span multiple organizational levels but requires guidance in navigating competing demands across levels.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can independently analyze programme stakeholder interests and influence across organizational levels, facilitate cross-stakeholder workshops, negotiate priorities between groups, and represent stakeholder needs to the programme team. Applies programme stakeholder engagement techniques effectively.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can manage complex, conflicting programme stakeholder relationships across organizational boundaries and hierarchical levels. Navigates political dynamics, power structures, and sponsor relationships with skill. Balances competing needs through negotiation and facilitation across the programme governance ecosystem. Builds trusted advisor relationships with senior leadership.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can represent stakeholder interests in multi-organizational, multi-cultural, or politically sensitive programme environments. Builds coalitions and consensus across diverse groups spanning portfolio, programme, and project levels. Anticipates stakeholder concerns before they surface. Designs engagement approaches for large, complex programmes.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Creates innovative programme stakeholder engagement frameworks and methodologies that advance how organizations manage multi-level stakeholder relationships. Recognized as an authority on programme stakeholder management. Shapes organizational culture around stakeholder-centricity in programme delivery.

narratives.name: Evolving Multi-Level Engagement from Ecosystem Mapping to Strategic Advocacy
narratives.description: Progression of programme stakeholder representation competency across five maturity levels.
citationNames: The Standard for Program Management -- Fourth Edition

narrativeContexts.context: Development of programme-level stakeholder representation competency requires foundational skills in empathy, active listening, structured facilitation, and an understanding of organizational power dynamics. Practitioners entering at the Basic level should recognize that programme stakeholders span multiple organizational levels -- from executive sponsors and governance boards through programme coordinators to operational staff who will sustain realized benefits -- creating a qualitatively more complex engagement landscape than single-project stakeholder management. Familiarity with stakeholder identification templates, interest-influence mapping, and engagement planning provides essential grounding. Organizational support through mentoring by experienced programme stakeholder managers, progressive exposure to multi-level engagement challenges, and opportunities to observe governance-level stakeholder interactions accelerates competency development.

Stakeholder representation competency develops through progressive exposure to increasingly complex multi-level stakeholder ecosystems. Basic practitioners identify stakeholder groups using standard templates, gather requirements across organizational levels, and document needs, requiring guidance when navigating competing demands between levels. At the Applies level, practitioners independently analyze stakeholder interests and influence across levels, facilitate cross-stakeholder workshops, negotiate priorities between groups, and represent stakeholder needs effectively. Mastery emerges when practitioners can manage complex, conflicting relationships across organizational boundaries and hierarchical levels, navigating political dynamics and sponsor relationships with skill while building trusted advisor relationships with senior leadership. The Adapts level represents the ability to represent interests in multi-organizational, multi-cultural, or politically sensitive environments, building coalitions and anticipating concerns before they surface. At the Innovating level, practitioners create innovative engagement frameworks that advance how organizations manage multi-level stakeholder relationships and shape organizational culture around stakeholder-centricity.

competencies.name: Communication
competencies.description: The ability to exchange information effectively across diverse audiences spanning multiple organizational levels, teams, and contexts, encompassing programme-level reporting, governance communication, cross-team facilitation, change communication, and the design of communication systems that keep all parties informed and aligned across the programme ecosystem.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Can communicate clearly in structured programme formats, participate effectively in programme meetings, and document programme information accurately. Understands the importance of audience-appropriate communication across organizational levels but may need guidance on tailoring messages to strategic, programme, and operational audiences.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can independently create effective programme communications for diverse audiences at multiple organizational levels. Facilitates cross-team meetings productively, presents programme information clearly, and practices active listening. Adapts communication style and medium to audience needs and programme context.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can design and implement comprehensive programme communication strategies for complex programmes with multiple stakeholder groups across organizational levels. Facilitates difficult cross-team conversations and governance negotiations effectively. Creates compelling programme narratives that influence strategic decision-making.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can design communication frameworks for large programmes and programme portfolios spanning organizational boundaries. Navigates crisis communication effectively under pressure. Coaches others in programme communication skills. Creates communication systems that enhance programme transparency and governance decision quality.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Creates innovative programme communication approaches, frameworks, and tools that advance how programme organizations share information and make decisions across organizational levels. Recognized as an authority on programme communication. Influences organizational communication culture in multi-project delivery.

narratives.name: Advancing Programme Information Exchange from Structured Reporting to Communication System Design
narratives.description: Progression of programme communication competency across five maturity levels.
citationNames: The Standard for Program Management -- Fourth Edition

narrativeContexts.context: Development of programme-level communication competency requires foundational skills in clear writing, structured presentation, active listening, and audience awareness. Practitioners entering at the Basic level should understand that programme communication spans multiple organizational levels -- strategic, programme, project, and operational -- each with distinct information needs, preferred formats, and engagement cadences. The ability to tailor messages for executive governance audiences seeking strategic-level reporting differs fundamentally from communicating with operational stakeholders requiring practical guidance on organizational change. Organizational support through exposure to programme communication challenges across levels, mentoring from experienced programme communicators, and access to programme reporting and facilitation tools accelerates competency development.

Communication competency at programme level develops through progressive exposure to increasingly complex multi-audience environments. Basic practitioners communicate clearly in structured programme formats, participate effectively in meetings, and document information accurately, though they may need guidance on tailoring messages across organizational levels. At the Applies level, practitioners independently create effective communications for diverse audiences, facilitate cross-team meetings productively, and adapt style and medium to audience needs. Mastery emerges when practitioners can design comprehensive communication strategies for complex programmes with multiple stakeholder groups, facilitate difficult cross-team conversations and governance negotiations, and create compelling narratives that influence strategic decision-making. The Adapts level represents the ability to design communication frameworks spanning organizational boundaries, navigate crisis communication under pressure, and create systems that enhance programme transparency and governance decision quality. At the Innovating level, practitioners create innovative communication approaches that advance how programme organizations share information and make decisions, influencing organizational communication culture in multi-project delivery.

competencies.name: Integration
competencies.description: The ability to coordinate across boundaries, manage cross-project dependencies, synthesize information from multiple sources, ensure architectural and organizational coherence, and create unified programme outcomes from diverse project contributions through systems thinking and cross-functional orchestration.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Can understand and track cross-project dependencies, support integration activities, and maintain dependency registers under guidance. Understands that programme-level integration spans technical, organizational, and process dimensions but requires supervision for complex integration challenges.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can independently facilitate cross-team coordination, manage dependency resolution for defined scope, and design integration mechanisms for small-to-medium programmes. Applies dependency visualization techniques (program boards, dependency maps) and categorization approaches (ROAM) effectively. Identifies integration risks and escalates appropriately.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can design and operate comprehensive integration frameworks for large, complex programmes spanning multiple teams, technologies, and organizational units. Facilitates large-scale planning events. Balances intentional architecture with emergent design. Applies systems thinking to identify non-obvious cross-project dependencies. Mentors others in integration practices. Adapts integration approaches to programme context and team maturity.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can establish organizational integration standards and practices for multi-programme or portfolio contexts. Designs integration approaches for novel situations (multi-site, multi-vendor, multi-methodology programmes). Coaches organizations in building integration capability. Identifies and resolves systemic integration challenges that span organizational boundaries.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Creates new integration frameworks, coordination techniques, and dependency management approaches that advance how organizations orchestrate complex multi-team delivery. Recognized as an authority on programme integration. Shapes industry thinking on scaled coordination, dependency management, and cross-boundary orchestration.

narratives.name: Building Cross-Boundary Orchestration Capability from Tracking to Thought Leadership
narratives.description: Traces the development of integration competency through progressive exposure to increasingly complex cross-boundary coordination challenges, from dependency tracking under guidance through industry thought leadership.

narrativeContexts.context: Development of integration competency requires foundational skills in systems thinking, cross-functional collaboration, and structured problem-solving. Practitioners entering at the Basic level should understand that programme-level integration spans technical (systems, architectures, interfaces), organizational (teams, roles, reporting lines), and process (workflows, cadences, handoffs) dimensions. Organizational support through exposure to progressively complex integration challenges, mentoring from experienced programme coordinators, and access to integration tools and frameworks is essential for advancement.

Integration competency develops through progressive exposure to increasingly complex cross-boundary coordination challenges. At Basic level, practitioners track dependencies and support integration under guidance. Applies-level practitioners independently facilitate coordination and manage dependency resolution. Mastery emerges when practitioners can design comprehensive integration frameworks, facilitate large-scale planning events, and apply systems thinking to identify non-obvious dependencies. The Adapts level represents capability to establish organizational integration standards and coach across organizational boundaries. Innovating represents thought leadership that advances how organizations orchestrate complex multi-team delivery through new frameworks and approaches.

competencies.name: Change Leadership
competencies.description: The ability to plan, lead, and sustain organizational transformation at programme scale, ensuring that programme capabilities are adopted and benefits realized through effective management of people, processes, culture, and the change network that bridges capability delivery and organizational adoption.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Can support change management activities, assist with communication plans, and contribute to training material development under guidance. Understands the importance of managing organizational change and the distinction between capability delivery and benefit realization but requires supervision for complex change challenges.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can independently plan and execute change management activities for defined stakeholder groups within a programme. Develops communication plans, conducts change readiness assessments, supports change champion networks, and tracks adoption metrics. Understands the outputs-capabilities-outcomes-benefits realization chain and its implications for change management.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can design and lead comprehensive change management strategies for complex programmes involving significant organizational transformation across multiple business units. Manages resistance, builds and activates change champion networks, advises governance on change progress and risks, and designs adoption measurement frameworks. Balances the rate of change delivery with the organization's capacity to absorb change.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can establish organizational change management capability for programmes, design change approaches for multi-organizational or deep cultural transformations, and develop change management methodologies for novel contexts. Anticipates change management challenges and designs proactive interventions. Coaches organizations in building sustainable change leadership capability.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Creates new change leadership frameworks and approaches that advance organizational transformation practice at programme scale. Recognized as an authority on managing organizational change through coordinated multi-project delivery. Shapes industry thinking on adoption, sustainment, and the organizational change dimension of programme management.

narratives.name: Developing Organizational Transformation Capability from Support to Industry Influence
narratives.description: Charts the development of change leadership competency through progressive exposure to increasingly complex organizational transformation challenges, from supporting change activities under guidance through industry thought leadership.
citationNames: The Standard for Program Management -- Fourth Edition

narrativeContexts.context: Development of change leadership competency requires foundational skills in empathy, communication, facilitation, and an understanding of human responses to change. Practitioners entering at the Basic level should recognize that organizational change is the bridge between capability delivery and benefit realization -- that without effective change management, programme capabilities remain unused and planned benefits are not realized. Organizational commitment to change management as a programme discipline (not an afterthought), and access to experienced change management mentors, is essential for advancement.

Change leadership capability develops through progressive exposure to increasingly complex organizational transformation challenges. Basic practitioners support change activities under guidance, assisting with communication plans and training materials. Applies-level practitioners independently plan and execute change management for defined scope, conducting readiness assessments and tracking adoption metrics. Masters design comprehensive change strategies for multi-business-unit transformations, managing resistance and building change champion networks. Adapts-level leaders establish organizational change management capability and design approaches for novel contexts. Innovating leaders advance the discipline through new frameworks that improve how organizations manage the human dimension of programme delivery.

narratives.name: From Strategic Investment Thesis to Confirmed Organizational Value
narratives.description: Traces the journey of a programme opportunity from initial strategic need identification through business case establishment, ongoing investment validation, and confirmed value realization.
citationNames: The Standard for Program Management -- Fourth Edition

narrativeContexts.context: Organizations operate within established strategic environments where latent market opportunities, competitive threats, and transformation possibilities coexist alongside operational routine. Strategic needs requiring coordinated multi-project delivery may be recognized informally but have not been formalized into an investment thesis with committed sponsorship. Individual projects may address isolated symptoms without recognizing the interconnected strategic opportunity that only a programme-level response can address.

A convergence of strategic drivers -- market shifts, regulatory requirements, competitive pressure, or technological disruption -- crystallizes a strategic need that demonstrably exceeds single-project scope. A programme sponsor emerges to champion the investment, articulating the business case with quantified benefits, risk assessment, and strategic alignment evidence. The governance body evaluates the investment against alternatives and authorizes the programme, transforming the opportunity from organizational aspiration into a funded, governed mandate with committed leadership and clear success criteria.

Throughout programme delivery, the original investment thesis faces continuous challenges as strategic context evolves, market conditions shift, and organizational priorities realign. The MSP "desirable, viable, achievable" test must be applied at each governance gateway, requiring analytical discipline and leadership courage to recommend continuation, restructuring, or termination based on evidence rather than sunk-cost thinking. The most dangerous moment comes when the opportunity has partially eroded or when benefit realization trajectories diverge from business case projections, demanding transparent governance reporting and strategic recalibration.

Measurable benefit realization confirms through objective evidence that the programme investment was strategically sound. The cumulative return on investment meets or exceeds the original business case, and stakeholders across the programme ecosystem acknowledge the strategic value delivered. The organization captures lessons about strategic investment decision-making, improving its capability to identify, assess, and pursue similar multi-project opportunities in the future. Unrealized and emergent opportunities identified during programme delivery are documented for potential future action, creating a feedback loop that enhances organizational strategic maturity.

narratives.name: Navigating the Multi-Level Programme Stakeholder Ecosystem
narratives.description: Describes the progressive engagement of a multi-level programme stakeholder ecosystem from initial mapping through active engagement strategy, alignment building, satisfaction confirmation, and relationship transition.
citationNames: The Standard for Program Management -- Fourth Edition

narrativeContexts.context: Programme stakeholder ecosystems span multiple organizational levels -- from executive sponsors and governance board members through programme coordinators and project team leads to operational staff who will ultimately adopt new capabilities and sustain realized benefits. This multi-level landscape introduces qualitatively different engagement challenges from single-project stakeholder management: competing priorities between governance bodies seeking strategic returns and business units experiencing the disruption of organizational change, information asymmetries between levels that distort decision-making, and the need to maintain sponsor commitment across multi-year programme timescales.

The programme must systematically map its stakeholder ecosystem across strategic, programme, project, and operational levels, establishing tailored engagement strategies for each level and building alignment mechanisms that translate diverse stakeholder needs into coherent programme direction. The engagement approach must balance the information needs of governance stakeholders (who require strategic-level reporting on benefits and risks) with the participation needs of operational stakeholders (who require practical guidance on how changes will affect their daily work and support during transition).

Progressive stakeholder engagement begins with comprehensive ecosystem mapping that identifies stakeholders across all four levels and assesses their interests, influence, and engagement requirements. An engagement strategy is established that provides differentiated communication channels and cadences for different stakeholder groups -- quarterly governance reviews for the programme board, monthly coordination briefings for project leads, and continuous change network engagement for operational stakeholders. Alignment is built through transparent reporting, facilitated negotiation of competing priorities, and the cultivation of programme champions who advocate for the programme within their communities.

When stakeholder engagement is managed as a multi-level, progressive discipline, programmes achieve stronger governance decision-making, higher organizational change adoption rates, and more sustainable benefit realization. The programme board makes informed strategic decisions based on accurate programme reporting. Business unit stakeholders become active participants in organizational change rather than passive recipients. Operational stakeholders transition from programme management to sustained business-as-usual ownership with the relationships and information needed for ongoing benefit protection.

narratives.name: From Strategic Promise to Sustained Organizational Value
narratives.description: Traces the benefits realization chain from project outputs through organizational capabilities and outcomes to measurable strategic benefits, illustrating the full lifecycle of programme value delivery.
citationNames: The Standard for Program Management -- Fourth Edition

narrativeContexts.context: Constituent projects within the programme produce tangible deliverables -- new information systems, redesigned processes, updated policies, training materials, organizational restructuring plans -- that represent the raw building blocks from which programme benefits will be constructed. These outputs are necessary but fundamentally insufficient for benefit realization: a deployed system that no one uses, a redesigned process that no one follows, or a training programme that changes no behavior produces zero strategic value regardless of the quality of the output itself.

When project outputs are combined with trained people who know how to use them, adapted processes that incorporate the new functionality, and organizational structures that support the new ways of working, organizational capabilities emerge. A capability represents what the organization can now do that it could not do before -- process customer orders digitally end-to-end, monitor platform performance in real time, or coordinate cross-regional teams through standardized interaction patterns. The transition from output to capability requires deliberate organizational change management: change champion networks that advocate for adoption, training programmes that build competence, and support structures that sustain early users through the transition period.

When capabilities are adopted and sustained by the organization, measurable changes in organizational behavior, performance, and effectiveness emerge as outcomes. Outcomes are observable behavioral changes: customer orders are actually processed digitally rather than merely being processable digitally, platform performance is actually monitored rather than merely being monitorable, cross-regional teams actually coordinate through standardized patterns rather than merely having the capability to do so. The gap between capability and outcome is where most programme benefit realization fails -- the assumption that adoption follows awareness is not supported by evidence.

Outcomes that are sustained over time produce the measurable strategic improvements that justify the programme investment. Financial benefits -- cost reduction, revenue growth, efficiency gains -- can be quantified against the baseline measurements established in the benefits realization plan. Strategic benefits -- market position improvement, regulatory compliance achievement, competitive advantage -- may require qualitative assessment alongside quantitative metrics. The benefits realized must be measured against the original business case to confirm return on investment, with emergent benefits and dis-benefits documented for organizational learning.

narratives.name: Bridging Strategy and Delivery Through Measurable Programme Outcomes
narratives.description: Describes the progressive management of programme objectives from strategic outcome definition through prioritization, cross-project achievement tracking, and post-programme evaluation.
citationNames: The Standard for Program Management -- Fourth Edition

narrativeContexts.context: Programme objectives operate at a different level of abstraction from project objectives: they express strategic outcomes (benefits delivered, capabilities established, organizational transformations achieved) rather than project deliverables (systems built, processes documented, teams trained). This creates a bridging challenge -- programme objectives must be specific enough to guide cross-project coordination decisions and measure progress, yet flexible enough to accommodate the strategic adaptation that multi-year programmes inevitably require. The gap between organizational strategy (which defines what must change) and project delivery (which produces the building blocks of change) requires programme objectives to serve as the connective tissue.

The programme must define objectives as measurable strategic outcomes traceable to organizational strategy, prioritize them to guide resource allocation and tranche sequencing, decompose them into constituent project targets while maintaining the coherent strategic thread, track cross-project progress toward shared objectives, and evaluate achievement against the original strategic intent -- adapting as context evolves while maintaining strategic coherence.

Programme objectives are defined collaboratively with governance stakeholders and expressed as strategic outcomes with measurable success criteria. Prioritization is performed through structured governance processes that make trade-offs explicit and allocate resources accordingly. Each programme objective is decomposed into constituent project objectives, with the mapping from project outputs to programme outcomes maintained as a living document. Progress is tracked through programme-level metrics that synthesize cross-project delivery data into objective achievement assessments reported at governance reviews.

Well-managed programme objectives provide the strategic coherence that transforms a collection of related projects into a coordinated programme. Governance bodies can make informed strategic decisions about programme direction based on objective achievement data rather than anecdotal project status. Resource allocation across projects is guided by objective priority rather than political influence. Stakeholders observe measurable progress toward the strategic outcomes that motivated the programme investment, building confidence and sustaining organizational commitment through multi-year delivery timescales.

narratives.name: Integrating Multi-Project Outputs into Coherent Programme Capability
narratives.description: Traces the journey of programme deliverables from initial capability envisioning through architectural definition, incremental integration, operational deployment, and sustained management.

narrativeContexts.context: Constituent projects operate as semi-independent delivery units, each producing outputs optimized for their individual scope and success criteria. Integration between project outputs is assumed rather than designed, and the gap between individual project deliverables and coherent organizational capability remains invisible until deployment reveals incompatibilities, gaps, and integration failures. The organization lacks an integrated view of how project outputs combine to create the capabilities described in the programme blueprint.

The programme blueprint articulates the target organizational capability that requires coordinated delivery from multiple projects. Architectural decisions define integration points, shared components, and technical standards that must govern individual project decisions. The programme must now orchestrate multiple project delivery streams toward an integrated capability that is greater than the sum of its parts -- requiring programme-level system demonstrations, integration testing, and architectural governance that individual projects cannot provide independently.

Integration challenges surface as project deliverables are combined: interface mismatches, conflicting architectural assumptions, quality inconsistencies, and timing dependencies create friction that threatens the coherence of the integrated capability. System demonstrations reveal gaps between the blueprint vision and actual delivery. The team-of-teams must resolve cross-project integration issues through collaboration, architectural compromise, and coordinated rework -- testing the programme's coordination mechanisms and the team-of-teams' collective commitment to shared outcomes over individual project objectives.

Integrated programme capabilities are deployed and operational, demonstrating through usage metrics and user feedback that the blueprint target state has been substantially achieved. Operational teams take ownership of sustained capability management, and continuous improvement processes ensure the capabilities evolve to meet changing organizational needs. The integration challenges encountered during delivery are documented as organizational learning, improving the organization's capability to orchestrate complex multi-project delivery in future programmes.

narratives.name: Orchestrating Cross-Project Coordination from Scoping to Closure
narratives.description: Documents the lifecycle of programme-level coordination work from initial scoping through organization, active execution, optimization, and orderly conclusion.
citationNames: The Standard for Program Management -- Fourth Edition

narrativeContexts.context: Programme-level coordination work can only be effectively scoped once the programme itself is defined -- with clear governance structures, identified constituent projects, and an established management approach. Prerequisites include an appointed programme manager with defined authority boundaries, an approved programme management plan documenting coordination responsibilities, and sufficient funding and resource allocation for the programme management function. The distinction between programme work (coordination, governance, integration, stakeholder management) and project work (delivery of specific outputs) must be understood by all participants before programme coordination work can begin.

Programme coordination work progresses through distinct phases aligned with the programme lifecycle. During programme definition, work focuses on establishing coordination mechanisms, governance processes, and reporting structures. During active delivery, coordination work intensifies around dependency management, cadence-based synchronization, integration oversight, and cross-project risk management. As the programme matures, coordination processes are optimized to minimize overhead while maintaining coordination effectiveness. During programme closure, work transitions to orderly handover, lessons capture, resource release, and formal closure activities. Throughout, the programme management function must continuously demonstrate value to constituent project teams -- the legitimacy of programme coordination work derives from the coordination value it provides, not from hierarchical authority.

narratives.name: Designing and Evolving the Team-of-Teams for Programme Delivery
narratives.description: Traces the journey of programme team design from initial organizational structure through formation, collaboration maturity, high performance, and intentional transition.

narrativeContexts.context: Before deliberate team-of-teams design, programme teams typically emerge from organizational convenience -- existing reporting structures, available headcount, and historical team boundaries -- rather than from intentional design aligned with programme architecture and value flow. Teams may be organized as component teams with high cross-team dependency, or as isolated project teams with no coordination mechanisms. Cognitive load distribution is unmanaged, resulting in some teams overwhelmed by too many responsibilities while others have insufficient scope to operate effectively. Cross-team coordination relies on informal relationships rather than designed interaction patterns.

The recognition that effective programme delivery requires deliberate organizational design drives the team-of-teams formation. Team Topologies provides the conceptual framework: four fundamental team types (stream-aligned, platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem) and three interaction modes (collaboration, X-as-a-service, facilitating) offer a design vocabulary for programme organizational architecture. SAFe's Agile Release Train provides the structural model: a long-lived, self-organizing team of teams (typically 50-125 people across 5-12 agile teams) that plan, commit, and deliver value together on a fixed cadence. The programme must now design its organizational structure as deliberately as it designs its technical architecture.

Team formation is just the beginning -- the journey from formed teams to a performing team-of-teams requires navigating significant challenges. Cross-team dependencies create friction and bottlenecks that test coordination mechanisms. Teams may resist programme-level standardization, preferring their established ways of working. Cognitive load imbalances emerge as delivery progresses and scope evolves. The tension between team autonomy and programme-level coherence requires continuous negotiation. Team topologies must evolve as the programme's coordination demands shift -- what worked during programme definition may not work during active delivery, and what works during stable delivery may not work during transition.

A mature team-of-teams delivers programme capabilities predictably and at sustainable pace, with cross-team coordination overhead minimized through structural improvements, practiced patterns, and evolved team topologies. Teams proactively identify and resolve cross-cutting issues without waiting for formal coordination events. When the programme concludes, team knowledge and capabilities are preserved through intentional transition, communities of practice continue beyond the programme, and organizational learning about team-of-teams design informs future programme organizational architecture. The organization's capability to design and operate effective multi-team structures has permanently improved.

narratives.description: Documents the iterative development of the programme operating model through PDCA cycles from initial principle agreement through establishment, use, refinement, and documentation as an organizational asset.

narrativeContexts.context: The programme leadership assesses the coordination requirements of its team-of-teams, considering factors such as team distribution, cadence preferences, tool ecosystem maturity, and organizational culture. Improvement hypotheses are formulated: "We believe that adopting cadence-based PI Planning with cross-team dependency visualization will result in improved delivery predictability and reduced dependency-related blockers because face-to-face alignment and explicit dependency identification have been shown to improve cross-team coordination in scaled environments." Success criteria include delivery predictability metrics, dependency resolution rates, and team satisfaction with coordination mechanisms.

The operating model is implemented with specific coordination events (PI Planning, system demos, inspect-and-adapt workshops), communication channels (programme-level Kanban, dependency boards, shared dashboards), and decision-making processes (escalation pathways, governance cadences). The implementation is observed for team adoption rates, event effectiveness, and unintended consequences. Deviations from the planned model are noted -- teams may adapt coordination events to fit their context, or communication channels may be supplemented with informal mechanisms.

After one or more coordination cycles (PIs, tranches, or equivalent), the programme evaluates operating model effectiveness against the original success criteria. Quantitative data -- delivery predictability, dependency resolution rates, cross-team lead times -- is compared with team satisfaction surveys and retrospective findings. The evaluation distinguishes between model design issues (the coordination approach itself is flawed) and implementation issues (the approach is sound but execution needs improvement).

Based on evidence, the programme makes explicit decisions: adopt successful elements into the standard operating model, adapt elements that show promise but need refinement, or abandon elements that demonstrably fail to add coordination value. Adopted elements are documented in updated coordination agreements and communicated to all teams. The improvement backlog is updated with hypotheses for the next improvement cycle, and operating model refinement becomes a continuous programme discipline rather than a one-time setup activity.

narratives.name: The Programme Lifecycle from Conception Through Coordinated Delivery to Orderly Closure
narratives.description: Documents the programme lifecycle from initial conception through formal definition, operational delivery, benefit transition, and orderly closure with organizational learning captured.
citationNames: The Standard for Program Management -- Fourth Edition

narrativeContexts.context: A programme can only be conceived when a strategic need or opportunity has been identified that demonstrably exceeds the scope of individual project management. Prerequisites include organizational recognition that coordinated multi-project delivery is required (the need cannot be addressed through independent project management or portfolio management), availability of a programme sponsor with sufficient authority to secure funding and organizational commitment, and initial identification of the constituent projects or workstreams that would form the programme. The MSP "desirable, viable, achievable" test provides the governance framework for assessing programme readiness: the programme must be desirable (aligned with strategy and delivering benefits that justify the investment), viable (achievable within resource and time constraints), and achievable (the organization has the capability to deliver and manage the programme).

The programme lifecycle progresses through six states that correspond to major lifecycle phases across the source frameworks. Conception and definition correspond to MSP's "Identifying a Programme" and PMI's "Programme Definition" phase, establishing the business case, governance, and management approach. Organization and initial delivery correspond to MSP's "Managing the Tranches" and SAFe's ART launch, with teams formed, governance operational, and constituent projects initiated. Active delivery corresponds to MSP's "Delivering the Capability" and "Realizing the Benefits" processes and SAFe's PI execution cycles, with coordinated project delivery producing integrated capabilities and measurable benefits. Transition and closure correspond to MSP's "Closing a Programme" and PMI's "Programme Closure" phase, with benefits transitioned to operational ownership, governance dissolved, and organizational learning captured. The typical programme duration spans 2-5 years, though SAFe's ART model operates as a semi-permanent structure with indefinite duration, and MSP's tranche-based approach allows programme boundaries to be reassessed at tranche boundaries (typically every 6-12 months).

narratives.name: Strategic Sequencing from Vision Through Adaptive Delivery to Fulfilment
narratives.description: Describes the progressive development and execution of the programme roadmap from initial high-level vision through detailed structuring, active execution, adaptive management, and completion.
citationNames: The Standard for Program Management -- Fourth Edition

narrativeContexts.context: Programmes face the strategic sequencing challenge of delivering multiple capabilities across multiple tranches while balancing the rate of capability delivery with the organization's capacity to absorb change. MSP structures delivery through tranches of 6-12 months each with governance gateways between them; SAFe connects roadmaps to PI Planning through a hierarchy spanning portfolio roadmap (12-24 months), solution roadmap (3-6 PIs), and PI roadmap (8-12 weeks). The roadmap must serve multiple audiences with different time horizons -- executives need strategic direction over years, programme leadership needs capability sequencing over quarters, and delivery teams need detailed planning over weeks.

The programme must create a strategic sequencing framework that connects organizational strategy to delivery execution, sequences benefit realization across tranches to build momentum and demonstrate value progressively, manages the balance between planning rigor and adaptability as strategic context evolves, and provides governance bodies with clear decision points at tranche boundaries. The roadmap must be the primary strategic planning instrument for the programme -- the living document that connects every coordination decision to the programme's strategic intent.

The roadmap is developed through collaborative planning involving governance stakeholders, programme leadership, and delivery teams. Initial envisioning establishes high-level capability milestones and benefit realization points aligned with strategy. Detailed structuring defines tranche scope, resource requirements, and review gates. During execution, progress is tracked against milestones and upcoming tranches are refined based on delivery learning. At tranche boundaries, governance reviews apply the "desirable, viable, achievable" test and approve or adjust the roadmap based on actual delivery experience, benefit realization progress, and evolving strategic priorities.

An effectively managed roadmap provides the programme with strategic coherence across multi-year delivery timescales. Governance bodies make informed tranche transition decisions based on clear criteria. Benefit realization is progressive -- early tranches deliver quick wins that build stakeholder confidence and organizational momentum. Stakeholders at all levels have visibility of programme direction and progress. The roadmap's overall effectiveness as a strategic planning instrument is assessed and lessons captured, improving the organization's capability to sequence and manage complex multi-project delivery in future programmes.
